Famous in battle

entries.origin: French and English, with Germanic roots

entries.meaning: Probably from Lucania

entries.meaning: Light
entries.note: Through Lucia, the feminine form of Lucius.

entries.meaning: Moon
From Middle English Laban, from Latin Laban, from Koine Greek Λάβαν (Lában), from Biblical Hebrew לָבָן (Lāḇān).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew of biblical origin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic لَبِيب (labīb, literally “sensible, reasonable”); this surname is predominantly found in Egypt.
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: From Lachlan + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lachlan.

entries.meaning: From Scottish Gaelic Lachlann, Lochlann (“land of the lochs, loch or fjord land, i.e. Scandinavia”), said to refer to an immigrant from Norway, a Norseman.
entries.note: A male given name from Scottish Gaelic mainly used in Scotland, recently also popular in Australia.
entries.origin: Scottish Gaelic mainly used in Scotland

entries.meaning: From Lachlan + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lachlan.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Medieval Latin Ladislaus, Latinization of a Slavic royal name *Voldislavъ, from the elements Proto-Slavic *voldь (“power”) (see *volděti) and Proto-Slavic *slava (“glory”). Doublet of Laszlo and Vladislav.
entries.note: A male given name from the Slavic languages.

entries.meaning: Unadapted borrowing from Latin Laetitia, laetitia (“happiness”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, a Latinate spelling of Letitia.

entries.meaning: French surname from Occitan, "the little beech tree".
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, originally in honor of the Marquis.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Lāgus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek Λᾶγος (Lâgos).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, of historical usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Manipuri ꯂꯥꯏꯈꯨꯔꯦꯝꯕꯤ (lāʼikhurembi).
entries.note: A female given name from Manipuri.

entries.meaning: Variant of Leila and Layla, from Arabic لَيْلَى (laylā), related to لَيْلَة (layla, “night”).

entries.meaning: Rare spelling variant of Leila.
entries.note: A female given name from Arabic, variant of Leila.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic لَيْث (layṯ).

entries.meaning: Derived from the noun lake.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit लक्ष्मण (lakṣmaṇa).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used mostly in India.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit लक्ष्मीदास (lakṣmīdāsa, “servant of Lakshmi”), from लक्ष्मी (lakṣmī, “the goddess Lakshmi”) + दास (dāsa, “servant, slave”).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek λᾰλᾰγή (lălăgḗ, “to prattle”).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Sanskrit ललित (lalita, “beautiful, lovely, graceful”).
entries.note: A male given name from Sanskrit used in India.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit ललित (lalita).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit commonly used in India.

entries.meaning: From a placename in Normandy, which was derived from Old French la mare (“the pool”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Lambert, from Old French Lambert, a saint's name (of a Bishop of Maastricht) brought to England by the Normans, from Proto-West Germanic *Landaberht, from *land (“land”) + *berht (“bright”). Cognate with Old English Landbeorht, Old High German Lantbërht, Dutch Lambrecht.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages; in modern use partly transferred back from the surname.

entries.meaning: African-American coinage.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, of late 20th and early 21st century African-American usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic, variant of Amin

entries.meaning: Short form of Alana, or from Russian Ла́на (Lána), diminutive of several names including Светла́на (Svetlána).
entries.note: A female given name from Russian.

entries.meaning: The surname is derived from a medieval given name Lanzo, short form of names beginning with the Germanic element *land; see land. Doublet of Lanzo.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages; by folk etymology associated with a lance. A diminutive of the male given name Lancelot.

entries.meaning: From Middle English Launcelot, from Old French Lancelot, from Frankish *Lanzo, hypocoristic form of names beginning in *Land-, from Proto-Germanic *landą (“land”), and diminutive Old French endings -el and -ot. Related to Old English Landbeorht (modern English Lambert).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: Two main origins: * Borrowed from Italian Lando, a patronymic surname from a personal name of Germanic origin. * Borrowed from Hungarian Landó, a pet form of the personal name Lándor.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Place names in England, from Old English lang (“long”) + dūn (“hill”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Modern re-spelling of Landon.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: As an English surname, from lane; as an Irish surname, from several origins, including Laighin. See Lane.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English lang (“long, tall”) + stan (“stone”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hawaiian Lani.
entries.note: A female given name from Hawaiian.

entries.meaning: A rare variant of Lakeisha.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, of African-American usage.

entries.meaning: Anglicized from Russian Ла́ра (Lára), a Russian pet form of Larissa, known from the novel (1957) and film (1965) Dr Zhivago.
entries.note: A female given name from Russian or Ukrainian.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic لاريج.
entries.note: A male given name from Arabic.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Ancient Greek Λάρισσα (Lárissa).
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek (after the mythological character and a 4th century Greek Orthodox martyr).

entries.meaning: The surname is a variant of the personal name Leonard. The city in Kansas is named after Fort Larned, which was named after Colonel Benjamin Larned.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from North Germanic, from Latin Laurentius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin occasionally given to Anglophones.

entries.meaning: Originally from a Middle English pet form of Lawrence + -son. In the United States, a common anglicization of the Swedish Larsson and Danish and Norwegian Larsen.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hungarian László, from the Slavic given name Ladislav, a variant of Vladislav. Doublet of Ladislaus.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit लता (latā, “creeper”).
entries.note: A female given name commonly used in India.

entries.meaning: From La- + Tanya.
entries.note: A female given name of African-American usage.

entries.meaning: La- + Tasha
entries.note: A female given name of African-American usage

entries.meaning: From Arabic لَطِيف (laṭīf, “gentle, kind”).

entries.meaning: From Arabic لَطِيف (laṭīf).

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Arabic لَطِيفَة (laṭīfa).
entries.note: A female given name from Arabic, masculine equivalent Latif.

entries.meaning: Possibly La- + Toya (“a Spanish pet form of Victoria”).

entries.meaning: Variant of Latoya.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin saint's name Laura, from the feminine form of laurus (“laurel tree”). A post-classical name made famous by Petrarch's sonnets to Laura in the fourteenth century.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From French Laureline. By surface analysis, Laurel + -ine.
entries.note: A female given name from French.

entries.meaning: An alteration of Laureline with -lyn.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Latin clipping of Laurentius. Doublet of Laurence.
entries.note: A unisex given name. A female given name from Latin, masculine equivalent Laurence; feminine of Lawrence

entries.meaning: From the name of a third century Roman martyr, Latin Laurentius, "a person from Laurentum", the place name possibly derived from laurus (“laurel”).
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, feminine equivalent Lauren.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Laurentius.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: An Italian pet form of Laura; first introduced into English as the name of one of the narrators in the Decameron.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Dzongkha ལའུ་རི་ (la'u ri).
entries.note: A less common spelling of Laurie, a diminutive of the female given name Laura.

entries.meaning: The given names are clippings of Laurence, Lawrence, Laura, or Lauren + -ie, all ultimately from Latin laurus (“laurel”). The surname is from the diminutive of Lawrence. The city in Missouri was named by its residents in 1961 after L. M. and William (Buster) Laurie, who in 1937 bought a building in the area and operated the Laurie Market, because of the goodwill generated by the family store over the years.
entries.note: A unisex given name. A diminutive of the male given names Laurence and Lawrence; alternative form of Lawrie; a pet form of the male given name Laurence or Lawrence.

entries.meaning: Alternative form of Lauren.
entries.note: A female given name, variant of Lauren.

entries.meaning: From Laura + -inda.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From the Italian surname, from a personal name derived from Latin laurus.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Spelling variant of Lauren.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit लावण्य (lāvaṇya, “beauty”).
entries.note: A female given name from Sanskrit commonly used in India.

entries.meaning: Variant of Laverne.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: 19th-century invention, possibly from the Californian town La Verne, named in the belief that it means "the green" in French. Laverne is a genuine French surname, from Gaulish la verne "the alder (tree place)" but - as in the case of Leroy - there is no apparent reason to turn it into an American given name.
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Latin Lavinia, of obscure meaning. Lavinium was a town in ancient Latium.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin used since the 17th century. It was fairly popular in the 18th and 19th centuries, but rare today.

entries.meaning: Clipping of Lawrence.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lawrence.

entries.meaning: See Laurence.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin, the usual spelling of Laurence in the U.S.; masculine of Lauren

entries.meaning: From Lawrence + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lawrence.

entries.meaning: From Middle English [Term?], from Old English [Term?], from hlāw (“hill, ound”) + tūn (“homestead”) (-ton).

entries.meaning: Rare spelling variant of Leila.
entries.note: A female given name from Arabic, variant of Leila.

entries.meaning: Topographic surname from lane.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: * (perseonal names): Derived from various place names in England.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Serbo-Croatian Lazar, ultimately from Ancient Greek Λάζαρος (Lázaros), from Hebrew אלעזר (ʼElʻāzār).
entries.note: A Serbian male given name from Serbo-Croatian.

entries.meaning: From Late Latin Lazarus, from Koine Greek Λᾱ́ζᾱρος (Lā́zāros), the given name of Biblical figures mentioned in Luke 16 and John 12, from Biblical Hebrew אֶלְעָזָר ('El'azár), a given name shared by various people in the Hebrew Bible and literally meaning "God has helped". Doublet of Eleazar.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hungarian László. Doublet of Vladislav.
entries.note: A male given name from Hungarian László

entries.meaning: From Hebrew לֵאָה (Le'a).
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Latin Leander, from Ancient Greek Λέανδρος (Léandros), from λεώς (leṓs) (Attic form of λᾱός (lāós, “people”)) + ἀνήρ (anḗr, “man”) + -ος (-os).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek, also of a Spanish sixth century saint.

entries.meaning: Variant of Leanne.

entries.meaning: A less common spelling variant of Leroy.

entries.meaning: From the name of a princess in the American fantasy film Star Wars (1977).

entries.meaning: From the nominative case of Old English lēah (“wood, meadow”), 'dweller by the wood or clearing'.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Various place names in England, Old English leac (“leek”) + tun (“settlement”), also in the sense of a herb garden.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hawaiian Leilani.
entries.note: A female given name from Hawaiian.

entries.meaning: Shortened from McLeland, McClellan, from Irish Mac Giolla Fhaoláin, "son of servant of (Saint) Faolán (=Little Wolf)".
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Hebrew לְמוּאֵל (lemu'él, ləmūʔel, literally “devoted to God”).
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew of biblical origin.

entries.meaning: The female name is from the Scandinavian, German and Russian pet form of Helena, Magdalena and Yelena (also spelled Elena). The river in Yakutia is from Russian Лена (Lena), from Evenki Елюенэ (Jeljujenə, “the Large River”). Compare to Yakut Өлүөнэ (Ölüöne). (Norwegian river): Probably related to Old Norse leir (“clay”) (see the references). (Town in Toten): From Old Norse lein.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin Lēnaeus (“Lenaeus”), from Ancient Greek Ληναῖος (Lēnaîos, “Lenaeus”), from ληναῖος (lēnaîos, literally “of or relating to the winepress”), from ληνός (lēnós, “winepress”) + -αῖος (-aîos).
entries.note: A male given name of historical usage

entries.meaning: From Irish Ó Leannáin (“descendant of Lover (Leannán)”) and from Ó Lonáin (“descendant of Blackbird (Lonán)”).
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname, of modern usage.

entries.meaning: Apheretic form of Eleanor.
entries.note: A female given name, variant of Eleanor.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Latin Leo and leo (“lion”), from Ancient Greek Λέων (Léōn) and λέων (léōn, “lion”), likely ultimately from a non-Indo-European language. Sometimes via other related languages such as French Léon and sometimes as a diminutive of related names such as Leonard and Leonardo.
entries.note: A male given name from Latin or Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From Leon + -a.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, a feminine form of Leo through Leon.

entries.meaning: From Old French Leonard, name of a 6th century Frankish saint, from Old High German leo (“lion”) or Old High German liut (“person”) and hart (“hard”). As a surname, also used as an anglicisation of Irish Ó Leannáin (Lennon).
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: From Leonard + -a.
entries.note: A female given name of rare usage.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Italian Leonardo.
entries.note: A male given name from Italian, equivalent to English Leonard.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Macedonian and Russian Леони́д (Leoníd) or Ukrainian Леоні́д (Leoníd), from Ancient Greek Λεωνίδας (Leōnídas). Cognate with the English historical name Leonidas.
entries.note: A male given name, a transliteration of a common East Slavic name (notably that of the first two Ukrainian presidents, Leonid Kravchuk and Leonid Kuchma, as well as Soviet leader Leonid Brezhnev).

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Λεωνίδᾱς (Leōnídās, “son of Leon / lion”).
entries.note: A male given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: From French Léonie, from Latin Leonia, feminine of Leonius, derived from leo (“lion”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: From the Italian short form of Eleonora, cognate to Eleanor.
entries.note: A female given name from Italian.

entries.meaning: Variant of Leonora. Compare Norah.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Leonore.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: From Old French Leopold, from Old High German liut (“people”) + bald (“bold”). The first part is sometimes associated by folk etymology with Latin leo (“lion”), as in Leo and Leonard. More at lede, bold.
entries.note: A male given name from the Germanic languages. Used in the 19th century but rare today.

entries.meaning: Possibly a variant of the modern Israeli name transliterated as Liora, from Hebrew, ליאורה "my light", or an American contraction of Leonora.
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Ancient Greek Λεπτίνης (Leptínēs).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Ancient Greek male given name Λεπτίνης (Leptínēs).

entries.meaning: Variant of Lakeisha.
entries.note: A female given name originating as a coinage, of African-American usage.

entries.meaning: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally Lesslyn, Scottish Gaelic lios cuileann (“garden of hollies”).
entries.note: A female given name transferred from the surname, used since the 18th century. Popular in the U.K. in the mid-20th century.

entries.meaning: From a placename in Aberdeenshire, originally Lesslyn, Scottish Gaelic lios cuileann (“garden of hollies”).
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: * As an English surname, from the placename Leicester. * Also as an English surname of Norman origin, from Lestre in Normandy, from Old French Lestra, from Medieval Latin Laxtra, perhaps from extera (“exterior (part of a property)”). * As an English and Scottish surname, variant of Lister. * Also as an English surname, variant of Laster. * As a Scottish and Irish surname, shortened from McLester.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of 19th century and later usage.

entries.meaning: Name of an obscure Spanish saint, Leticia, from Latin laetitia "gladness".
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, popular in medieval England; rather rare today.

entries.meaning: A medieval vernacular form of Letitia.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, variant of Letitia.

entries.meaning: From Letitia + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Letitia or Lettice.

entries.meaning: From Letitia + -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Letitia.

entries.meaning: Ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (lēwî), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Lewi.
entries.note: A male given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Russian Левин (Levin), from Леви (Levi) + -ин (-in, “forming possessives & adjectives”), ultimately from Biblical Hebrew לֵוִי (“Levi”), of uncertain origin. Doublet of Levine.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: From the biblical name Levi. Unlike the biblical spelling, which descended through continuous liturgical traditions that preserved final secondary stress (causing it to shift to IPA⁽ᵏᵉʸ⁾: /ˈliːvaɪ/), the surname was re-introduced into English after the 1650s via French Lévy and German Levy.
entries.note: A male given name.

entries.meaning: Diminutives: Lewis + -y
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lewis.

entries.meaning: A short form of Alexa or Alexandra.
entries.note: A female given name from Ancient Greek.

entries.meaning: Clipping + -ie.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Alexis, Alexia, Alexandra, and Alexandria.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Turkish Leya and Arabic لَيْيَا (layyā).
entries.note: A female given name from Turkish or Arabic.

entries.meaning: From the name of the River Lea + Old English tūn (“enclosure; settlement, town”). Doublet of Luton.
entries.note: A unisex given name, sometimes regarded as a variant of Leighton.

entries.meaning: From liberty.
entries.note: A unisex given name. A female given name from English.

entries.meaning: From Lydia + -y with phonetic respelling.
entries.note: A pet form of the female given name Lydia.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Liesel.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given name Elisabeth, from German.

entries.meaning: Altered respelling of Lawrence.
entries.note: A surname transferred from the given name.

entries.meaning: Shortening of Lilian or Lillian.

entries.meaning: From Sanskrit लीला (līlā, “play, charm”).

entries.meaning: Short form of Delilah; also a variant of Leila.
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Latin lilia, plural of lilium (“lily”), or a Latinization of the English Lily.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin lilium (“lily”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: First recorded in 16th-century Scotland, a variant of Lilian or possibly from the Spanish Liliosa, name of a 9th-century saint, both ultimately from Late Latin lilium (“lily”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from Hebrew לִילִית (lîlîṯ).
entries.note: A female given name from Hebrew.

entries.meaning: From Macedonian Лилјана (Liljana), from лилјан (liljan).
entries.note: A transliteration of the Macedonian female given name Лилјана (Liljana), equivalent to Lilian

entries.meaning: Used since the sixteenth century, possibly originally a pet form of Elizabeth, but generally accepted as a variant of Late Latin lilium (“lily”).
entries.note: A female given name from Latin, of American usage; variant form Lilian (UK).

entries.meaning: A less common form of Liliana.
entries.note: A female given name from Latin.

entries.meaning: Variant of Liliana, or from Lily + Anna.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Transliteration of Bulgarian Лиляна (Liljana), equivalent to English Lilian.
entries.note: A female given name from the Slavic languages.

entries.meaning: From Lily + Anna.
entries.note: A female given name.

entries.meaning: Short form of any female name ending in -lina, such as Angelina, Carolina, Evelina. It can also be construed as a rare feminine form of Linus.
entries.note: A female given name, occasionally used in English.

entries.meaning: Shortening.
entries.note: A diminutive of the male given name Lincoln.

entries.meaning: Inherited from Middle English Lincolne, from Old English Lincolle, Lindcolen, Lindcylene, from Latin Lindum Colōnia (“the Roman settlement Lindum Colonia”), from Proto-Brythonic *llɨnn (“pool”), from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”), in reference to the Brayford. In the United States, many of the places established since 1865 are named after Abraham Lincoln.
entries.note: A male given name transferred from the surname, of American usage, originally in honor of Abraham Lincoln.

entries.meaning: Latinised short form of Germanic compound names ending in -lind, -linde (“tender, soft”) (English -inda), such as Sieglinde and Dietlinde, and earlier names such as Old High German Irmilinda and Old Dutch Frithelind, from Proto-Germanic *linþaz (“gentle, mild”), whence also Old English līþe (“gentle, mild, pliable, limber”) (English lithe). Later misassociated with unrelated Spanish linda (“beautiful”).
entries.note: A female given name from the Germanic languages.

entries.meaning: * As a Dutch, German and Jewish surname, plural form of Linde. * As a Dutch and West Flemish surname, from several placenames called Linden or Lienden. Also shortened from Vanderlinden. * As a Swedish surname, from lind (“lime tree”). Compare Lindeen. * As an English surname, variant of Lindon. * As an Irish surname, shortened from McLinden, itself a variant of McClinton.
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname, or for the linden tree.

entries.meaning: From Lindsey in Lincolnshire, from Old English Lindesēġe, Lindesīġe (“Isle of Lind”), the Old English name of the city of Lincoln, Lincolnshire, in which "Lind" comes from the Common Brittonic form of the name of Lincoln and "isle" refers to Lincoln being surrounded by fenland; from Proto-Brythonic *llɨnn (“pool”), from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”), in reference to the Brayford + Old English ēġ (“island”); c…
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname. A male given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: From Old English Lindesege, ultimately from Proto-Brythonic *llɨnn (“pool”), from Proto-Celtic *lindos (“lake, liquid”) (as in Lincoln) + Old English ēġ (“island (of land)”).
entries.note: A unisex given name transferred from the surname.

entries.meaning: Diminutives with -y.
entries.note: A diminutive of the female given names Linda, Lindsay, and Linnet.

entries.meaning: In modern use a spelling variant of Lynette, though it is also identical with a rare French name, diminutive of Line, from Caroline, Pauline and other female names ending in -line.
entries.note: A female given name from Welsh.

entries.meaning: Borrowed from German Lorelei (“murmuring rock or lurking rock”), but not used as a given name in Germany. The Lorelei (or Lorelei, Loreleï, Lore Lay, Lore-Ley, Lurley, Lurelei, Lurlei) is an infamous maritime disaster site because of the Rhine's current and the surrounding terrain. The shipwrecks have been subject to mythological explanation attempts since around 900 AD.
